content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published a document in March 2015 titled Rapid Guidance on the Decommissioning of Ebola Care Facilities. This document was created in collaboration with the governments of Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, as well as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Infection Control Africa Network (ICAN), and UNICEF. The guidance is based on current evidence and expert opinion, aiming to assist national governments and partners in safely decommissioning Ebola care facilities. The document emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material do not imply any opinion on the legal status of countries, territories, or boundaries. Maps included in the publication may show approximate borderlines where full agreement has not been reached. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information, but the material is distributed without warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. The 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa was the largest in history, with nearly 25,000 cases reported in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone as of March 2015. In response to the urgent need for treatment beds, many facilities were repurposed or newly constructed to isolate and treat patients. As the number of new cases declined, strategies were needed to scale down activities and bed capacities in these facilities, which included Ebola treatment units, community care centers, and isolation centers. The closure or repurposing of these facilities must follow evidence-based best practices while considering the social and psychological impact of the outbreak on affected populations. A major challenge in decommissioning these facilities is decontamination, which involves reducing microbial contamination to eliminate the risk of disease transmission. The process may range from cleaning with soap and water to sterilization. The guidance highlights the importance of minimizing environmental, health, safety, and social risks during decontamination and repurposing. A high degree of care is required to ensure the safety of staff and individuals accessing the facilities after decontamination. The document also reviews existing evidence on the survival of the Ebola virus on surfaces, in water, and in sanitation infrastructures. The Ebola virus is not a fecal-oral pathogen, and there is no reported transmission via water. The virus is fragile in the environment, with its infectivity and virulence declining rapidly under tropical conditions. Studies indicate that the virus has a relatively short survival time on surfaces at temperatures common in tropical settings (20°C or greater). For example, no viable virus was recovered from glass or plastic surfaces after two days at room temperature. The virus is also sensitive to ultraviolet light and drying. Regarding feces and urine, evidence suggests that the Ebola virus is not frequently present in the excreta of infected patients and declines rapidly under tropical conditions. Most fecal matter from Ebola care facilities did not contain the virus. Studies have shown that the virus is inactivated within days in feces and sewage due to microbial activity and higher temperatures during natural biodegradation. The outer lipid membrane of enveloped viruses, such as Ebola, is highly sensitive to physical, chemical, and biological agents, leading to a loss of infectivity. The guidance underscores the importance of water and sanitation services in protecting human health during disease outbreaks, including Ebola. These services are critical for infection prevention and control (IPC) practices, particularly to prevent concurrent outbreaks of fecal-oral diseases. The document provides an overview of measures for planning, demolition, and completing the decontamination of Ebola care facilities, ensuring the safety and repurposing of infrastructures and resources used during the outbreak.
